## **Climate Change, Industrial Solar, and the Globalized Local in Joshua Tree, California**

Jennifer M. Bernstein University of Hawai‘i at Manoa

## **ABSTRACT**

In their native habitat, Joshua trees ( _Yucca brevifolia_ ) are threatened by global climate change. Increased temperature fluctuation and prolonged drought have diminished the tree’s southern range, and scientists anticipate that Joshua Tree National Park may ultimately lose up to ninety percent of its population. The Morongo Basin, in which Joshua Tree National Park is situated, has been targeted as prime territory for alternative energy development. Given that alternative energy offsets carbon emissions, increased development would alleviate pressure on Joshua trees (as well as countless other species). So why do many residents of the Joshua Tree region oppose alternative energy development? This paper argues that local opposition to solar development is due to the way climate change is perceived psychologically, issues with the solar installations themselves, and the tendency to think utopian locally and dystopian globally. The local is characterized as a place of care, stewardship, and freedom, while the global is portrayed as corporate and placeless. Minimizing the relationship between the local and the global hides the transportation, telecommunication, and human networks that fundamentally enable the “sense of place” that Joshua Tree residents value. Invoking the framework of eco-cosmopolitanism, this paper suggests that attention to scale and interconnectedness may engender an environmental ethic able to address both local and global environmental concerns.

## **Background**

In public opinion polls, Americans regularly exhibit concern for the environment. In March of 2013, fifty percent of Americans agreed (vs. forty-one percent who disagreed) that the environment should be given priority even if it hampers economic growth (Jacobe 2013). While Americans typically rank concern about global warming as low when compared to other issues, they report their level of worry to be increasing: The percentage of respondents

worrying “a great deal” increased from fifty-one percent in 2011 to fifty-five percent in 2012 to fifty-eight percent in 2013 (Saad 2013). Additionally, Americans are largely supportive of solar power. In a recent Gallup poll, solar outranked other alternative energy sources when respondents were asked where the U.S. should put its emphasis. Moreover, solar was supported by a large majority in each political party, and more so in the West (seventy-nine percent) than in other regions of the country (Swift 2014). Broad support for solar across political and sociodemographic groups explains, in part, the degree of backing it receives from politicians. President Obama’s Clean Power Plan, introduced in April of 2015, was dubbed “bold and absolutely necessary” by California Governor Jerry Brown, even though the carbon emissions guidelines in Obama’s plan are less stringent than those already in place in California (Barboza 2015). National environmental organizations like the Sierra Club, The Wilderness Society, and the National Resources Defense Council have all publicly supported utility-scale solar initiatives as a means of reducing reliance on fossil fuels.

In southeastern California’s high desert, the “census designated place” (CDP) of Joshua Tree is located in what seems like an ideal region for solar development. The larger Morongo Basin is subject to competing uses, including BLM-designated wilderness, U.S. Forest Service-designated wilderness, state land conservation, and the Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center. The town itself has a footprint of ninety-five square miles and a population of approximately 7,400 “artists, musicians, working families, businesspeople, telecommuters and retirees” (Joshua Tree Chamber of Commerce, n.d.). Residents are largely Caucasian, high-school educated, and split politically, with thirty-two percent registered Democrat, thirty-three percent Republican, and twenty-six percent with no party affiliation. The population is underemployed but not unemployed, with an unemployment rate of 4.7 percent and a poverty rate of twenty-one percent (U.S. Bureau of the Census, 2000). Over eighty percent of the community has a per-capita income of less than $75,000, with nearly twenty percent employed by the government (including 665 residents employed directly by Joshua Tree National Park). Absent are high-end manufacturing, technology, and/or service industry firms. There seem to be two logical options for increasing economic development in the region: alternative energy and tourism.

Joshua Tree residents perceive the town as distinct from surrounding communities, which both affirms the “sense of place” of locals and benefits the tourist economy. The local Chamber of Commerce proudly advertises

“art galleries, a yoga studio...great vegan fare...and a Certified Farmers Market right in town” (Joshua Tree Chamber of Commerce, n.d.).

“There are not many towns like this left...it is one of those towns that has yet to be overrun and gentrified,” said resident Ryon Weber (Roth 2015). Rural communities have been found to identify strongly with local places, both the topography/ecology as well as more abstract personal attachments (Ching and Creed 1997). Residents also tend to depend more heavily on the natural-resource base, and harbor distinct normative views about human-environment interactions (Hamilton et. al 2013). When residents of the Morongo Basin were asked in 2008 about what constitutes “Morongo Basin Treasures,” they overwhelmingly responded with aspects of the biophysical environment, with Joshua Tree National Park coming in first, followed up by “my backyard.” Also mentioned were “clean and clear daytime skies,” “view and vistas from mountains and hills,” and “clear and open ridgelines” (Sonoran Institute 2012). A local couple who considers themselves “new homesteaders” explained their move to the area as explicitly seeking to escape the “urban apartments we spent our adult lives in (and) the suburbs we grew up in,” and go “off the grid” and become “embedded in slightly settled, mostly unfenced quiet wilderness, with deep unsmogged horizons, enveloped nightly by a fantastically starred sky” (Babcock 2013). Local environmental groups seek to protect Joshua Tree’s “sense of place.” Due in part to grass roots efforts, bobcat trapping was banned in August of 2015. At present, local groups are opposing a plan by the Bureau of Land Management to allow increased levels of off-road vehicle access in the Western Mojave region. In October 2015, community members came out in support of a proposal to designate three new National Monuments in the area (Mojave Trails, Sand to Snow, and Castle Mountains National Monument), citing outdoor recreation and wildlife habitat amongst their reasons for supporting more land being transferred to the federal government (Cart 2015).

A major threat to the ecology of the area is global climate change, which has a particular deleterious effect on the Joshua tree ( _Yucca brevifolia_ ) itself (Davidson 2015). A recent survey of the park showed that the Joshua Tree has been eliminated from nearly thirty percent of its historic range. Climate change will affect the tree even more dramatically in the future: Models using a 5.4°F change in temperature show the tree’s range being reduced nearly ninety percent within the park, growing in small islands rather than the dramatic stands visible today. Juvenile Joshua trees are affected more,

due to their immature root structure; while older trees need a soaking only every few years, young trees require regular rain events to survive. And even if rainfall follows historic patterns, increases in temperature mean increases in evaporation, making less water available to the plants (Davidson 2015). Compounding this problem is the nonnative and highly flammable red brome grass, the growth of which is fueled by windblown nitrogen from Southern California. This has increased the frequency and severity of fires in the region. The problem is so acute that the environmental group WildEarth Guardians is petitioning the Fish and Wildlife Service to designate the Joshua tree a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act. The desert tortoise, listed as threatened, is already suffering the effects of long-term drought (Roth 2015d). The reduction of carbon emissions would have a positive impact on the Joshua tree and other species critical to the ecological functioning of the region.

One means of reducing carbon emissions is alternative energy, and the California desert is home to a number of renewable energy projects. Along with four other counties, San Bernardino County applied for and received a Renewable Energy Conservation and Planning Grant from the Department of Energy, indicating a regional commitment to renewable energy development. Further, San Bernardino County is part of the statewide Desert Renewable Energy Conservation Plan (DRECP), which seeks to “provide effective protection and conservation of desert ecosystems while allowing for the appropriate development of renewable energy projects” (DCREP, n.d.). The San Gorgonio Pass Wind Farm, located on Interstate 10 about thirty miles west of the town of Joshua Tree, is the oldest wind farm in the United States, with approximately 2,700 windmills delivering 615mw of power (Breeding 2013). In nearby Riverside County, the Desert Sunlight Solar Farm covers nearly 4,000 acres. This solar farm is unique because of the state and federal government’s support of its development. Not only is it situated on federal land, but the project developers also received a $1.46 billion loan from the U.S. Department of Energy. While government support for solar has waned in recent years, recently both state governor Jerry Brown and President Obama publicly recommitted themselves to renewable energy (Goldstein 2015). Given residents’ strong attachments to the local landscape, as well as the need for employment opportunities, one might imagine that the local “alternative energy” economy would be welcomed with open arms. But despite the environmental benefits, state and federal support, and longstanding precedent of alternative energy development in the region,

industrial solar has faced numerous obstacles in the Joshua Tree area. Recently, two solar installations failed to get approval. In Landers, just to the north of Joshua Tree, a 3mw installation was ultimately rejected by the Board of Supervisors, due in part to local opposition. The installation was proposed by the sustainable energy company sSolar, and many residents argued that the plant would be out of place in a residential neighborhood and mar the “pristine desert ecosystem” (Nelson 2015). sSolar suggested that the development would have created seventy jobs, though a local environmental group opposed to the project states that these jobs would not have used local labor (The Landers Association, n.d.). A 20mw plant at the site of a former airport near 29 Palms, proposed by NextEra solar, is also facing controversy. The reception by local residents has been largely negative, with concerns about avian death, elimination of a potentially functional airport, and a lack of economic benefits for local residents (Schauppner 2015). Buck Buckley, who generates income by renting a vintage trailer to tourists, opposes the development on the basis that tourists come to see “unspoiled, unchanged, open space, which they don’t have in large cities” (Roth 2015c). Overall, the area is rapidly gaining a reputation as a challenging place for solar development proposals.

Local opposition to solar development can be explained by three main factors. The first is the way climate change is perceived psychologically, which is more complex than “NIMBYism” and impedes voluntary sacrifice for what is seen as a distant problem. Second are issues with the solar installations themselves, which have eroded public trust. Finally, there is the issue of scale. Opposition to industrial-scale solar is consistent with the tendency to “think utopian locally and dystopian globally” (Proctor and Berry 2011), despite the multiple scales interacting at any place at any point in time. This runs counter to the history of the region, which has long been at the intersection of economic and cultural flows.

## **Barriers**

Local opposition to industrial-scale solar is often attributed to “NIMBYism,” or “not in my backyard” syndrome, but this explanation is limited at best. NIMBYism is characterized by five factors: distrust of project managers, concern about risk, limited information about project specifics, emotional responses, and a prioritization of the local over the global. But studies have shown that the factors do not always cohere: While in one case there may be distrust of project sponsors, it is not always accompanied by emotional

responses or localized attitudes (Kraft and Clary 1991). Morongo Basin residents, for example, do not lack information about project specifics. Further, NIMBYism has not always proved to be a predictive variable. In a study of support for offshore oil drilling, researchers in Santa Barbara found other factors correlated more strongly than proximity, namely environmentalism and political party (Smith et. al 2004). Traditionally, NIMBYism is seen when there are public health risks caused by facilities with _negative_ environmental impacts—typically hazardous waste, nuclear power, and toxins (Slovic 1987)—whereas parties on both sides of the solar installation controversies claim pro-environmental objectives. Thus, while NIMBYism may begin to explain attitudes surrounding solar in the Joshua Tree area, it does not tell the whole story.

Research has shown that the public generally sees the effects of climate change as occurring in the distant future, while the costs of addressing climate change are felt immediately. Construal Level Theory (CRT) describes four aspects of psychological distance, including spatial, temporal, hypotheticality, and distance between observer and social target (Lieberman and Trope 2002). Global climate change is seen as distant in all of these aspects. In the comments section of a _Desert Sun_ newspaper article, resident David Fick wrote, “There are no benefits for the local communities hosting industrial solar farms. The conditions have already been set: property values and taxes go down, local water supplies get used, view sheds downgrade, local rooftop generated energy gets displaced and prevented, migratory birds die, dust increases, more transmission lines for the landscape...what’s to like about any of this?” (Schauppner 2015). The lack of economic benefits for residents is often explicitly mentioned. “Why would we want to have our homes devalued so you can make a profit and we lose?” said Yucca Mesa resident Elizabeth Karman at a public hearing about a proposed solar development by NextEra (Schauppner 2015). The reduction of greenhouse gas emissions is unmentioned, indicating mental distance from the minds of residents. Studies regarding the impacts of global climate change on Joshua trees are temporally distant (i.e., tree mortality will increase by 2050), making residents unmotivated to sacrifice view sheds (and the tourism that accompanies them) in the short term. Additionally, climate change is abstract and technical, making it seem even less urgent (Weber 2006). This is in comparison to places like Maine, for example, where the impacts of climate change are already apparent in the local fishing and tourism industries (Kraus n.d.).

A second barrier is that industrial solar has over-promised and underdelivered. Procedural delays, technology issues, and plants not operating at capacity have exacerbated opposition from local citizen groups. The DRECP itself has faced hurdles, including critique from the EPA that the plan overestimates the amount of renewable energy that could be generated from the region and fails to specify whether development would take place on already disturbed land. The Ivanpah Solar Electric Generating System covers 5.5 miles of Mojave Desert to the north of Joshua Tree with concentrated solar power. BrightSource Energy Inc., the lead developer of the project, was backed by investors like Google and NRG Energy and a $1.6 billion loan from the Department of Energy, and predicted that the plant would produce 1 million mw of energy per year. Since, the project has struggled to operate at anywhere near that capacity. As permitting and environmental regulations slowed the development process, the profitability of solar declined and concentrated solar power became increasingly obsolete. Plus, concentrated heat in the region causes avian mortality, as birds literally ignite in the “solar flux” above the panels (Ucar 2015). Even more of a debacle is the Palen Solar plant, that German-based Solar Millennium stated would produce 500mw of electricity using “parabolic trough” technology. Though the project was initially approved by the California Energy Commission in 2011, Solar Millennium filed for bankruptcy in 2012. BrightSource Energy then bought the plant, changing the technology to “power tower” and reducing the estimated output to 250mw of electricity. This modification included two 750-foot towers, so BrightSource partnered with the Spanish firm Abengoa, which specializes in tower construction. The National Park Service opposed the project, citing “unavoidable and unmitigatable significant adverse impacts” on visibility and wildlife (Clarke 2013). The controversial towers prompted the California Energy Commission to reject the proposal. BrightSource/ Albengoa modified the proposal and reapplied, and ultimately the CEC approved one of the 250mw towers. Surprisingly, BrightSource/Albengoa rescinded their proposal, citing their inability to build the plant in time to qualify for a thirty percent government tax credit that was due to expire at the end of 2016. But Albengoa then bought out BrightSource, affirming their commitment to the project regardless of whether or not they received a tax credit and abandoning the controversial towers in favor of the original “parabolic trough” technology. The deadline to start building was extended by the CEC. In yet another twist to the saga, in December of 2015 Albengoa applied for bankruptcy in Spain and the plan looked all but dead. However,

as of January 2016, Albengoa was in negotiations to sell Palen to EDF Renewable Energy. Under the San Diego-based company’s ownership, “traditional” solar panels would be used and the controversial towers abandoned (Roth 2015a). This has assuaged the fears of some environmentalists about visibility and bird mortality, but concern remains about the effect on sensitive species of wildlife (Roth 2015b). All together, the public bumbling of solar companies and the consistent underperformance of existing plants have eroded public trust.

Third is the issue of scale. Climate change takes place at the global scale, which can seem too large, abstract, and difficult to impact positively. This scale discrepancy is not lost on researchers: “Climate change is an international issue,” states Cameron Barrows of UC Riverside. “The folks on the ground, the land managers at [Joshua Tree National Park], don’t have the ability to fix that” (Davidson 2015). Citizen groups portray industrial solar as appropriate at certain scales and inappropriate at others. The Landers Association website states, “Solar power itself is definitely a good source of electric power to replace coal, oil and other fossil fuels to generate electricity and the State of California has a goal of having 30% of the state’s electricity generated by renewables by 2020. Our problem with this (project in Landers) is that it is located in the middle of a rural residential community” (The Landers Association, n.d.). Other issues that have received media attention, such as the clearing of Joshua trees in Antelope Valley to make way for solar development, clearly pit the local against the global (Carlile 2015). One scale is not superior, but rather processes are operating at multiple scales simultaneously. Focusing on one scale and not others leads to a partial understanding of the social, political, and environmental factors affecting the situation.

The prioritization of the local over the global is regularly invoked in antisolar campaigns. “There are no benefits for the local communities hosting industrial solar farms,” states resident David Fick (Schauppner 2015). But David Harvey has argued that the local is not innocent (Harvey 1996). By invoking the local, regional opinions are essentialized and homogenized. The local is regularly portrayed as a place of trust, care, and goodness, and revered as a counter-hegemonic force to globalizing influences (Hinrichs and Kremer 2002). State DuPuis and Goodman (2005): “If the global is domination then in the local we must find freedom” (p. 361). The narrative of rapacious global capital versus the pure local underlies much of the antisolar rhetoric. On his “Defend Joshua Tree” blog, Jay Babcock (himself a

relatively recent transplant) states: “more than a hundred acres of pristine north Joshua Tree desert wilderness have already been scraped, fenced off and covered in solar panels by Sun Edison Solar to prop up an [expletive] energy strategy” (Babcock 2015). Further, what is defined as best for local communities is explicitly curated and its boundaries are policed. This is demonstrative of what Childs (2003) calls ‘‘the politics of conversion,’’ when a small group, after determining what is ideal for a larger group of people, attempts to convert others to accept and advocate for their vision of utopianism. In Joshua Tree this includes yoga studios but not off-road vehicles, vacation rentals but not Dollar Stores, multi-acre art installations but not solar panels. “The local” is itself a social construction, an act of normative decision-making by a particular group.

Rather than remain limited to a carefully constructed idea of local, the town of Joshua Tree must be thought of as a hub or node within a much larger network, since a place cannot be understood without situating it within the broader institutional context. Doreen Massey (1994) calls this a “global sense of place.” One major federal influence on Joshua Tree is its geographic proximity to Joshua Tree National Park. This has both biological and economic implications. For one, the park serves as a sanctuary and migratory corridor for plants and wildlife. Economically, it provides a base for consistent and permanent flows of tourists (1.6 million visitors in 2015) and who also needed places to eat and sleep (Steinberg 2015). This influx has been capitalized on by residents, who are threatened by the adverse affects of solar development on the quirky desert accommodations they offer on rental sites like Airbnb. Hosting out-of-town guests is portrayed as more than a source of income; rather, it is spreading the gospel of wilderness. Babcock advises, “Look for the stars, or some other overwhelming natural/ wild feature, buy property there, and steward it wisely. Share it with naturedeprived urban folks via vacation rentals” (Babcock 2013). Of course, visitors to Babcock’s also want their wild places complete with wireless high-speed Internet. And sharing wild nature with nature-deprived urban folks is one of the few profitable ventures in the area, with tourists spending approximately $19 million on lodging in the area in 2013 (Steinberg 2015).

But perhaps the biggest elephant in the room is the city of Los Angeles, a mere 130 miles (a two-hour drive) away. Long Beach resident Ben Sasso stated: “[Joshua Tree is] a relief valve from the congestion. It’s a place to explore and escape from L.A.” (Steinberg 2015). Flows of people from Los Angeles have long shaped the region, and their continued presence denies

any idealized conception of the town as immune from globalizing forces. Pioneertown, just outside of Joshua Tree, was built in 1946 as a film set because it is within a reasonable drive of production firms based in the city. Los Angeles’ music scene has always boomeranged off of Joshua Tree, with “open mic” nights at Pappy and Harriet’s Roadhouse in Pioneertown and vinyl music stores in Yucca Valley, not to mention the ghost of Graham Parsons at the Joshua Tree Inn.

Songwriter Ted Quinn states: “I had to get out of Los Angeles,” a move that led to the founding of Radio Free Joshua Tree, a station that features artists from, or who have ties to, the area (Fleishman 2015). It has also become a refuge for visual artists. Andrea Zittell, Noah Purifoy, Jason Rhoades, and others have found solace and inspiration in the area, and collectors have followed. “Joshua Tree is like the art world’s Palm Springs,” said Lisa Overduin in a _New York Times_ interview.  Beyond the cultural amenities provided by Angelenos, there is the practicality of income. The number of residents earning $75,000 to $99,000 in the Joshua Tree CDP increased from six percent in 2000 to nearly fourteen percent in 2014 (U.S. Bureau of the Census 2000), likely due to an increase in Los Angeles-based telecommuters. States Babock (2013): “Telecommuting gives us some income, and the cost of living here is lower than anywhere else we’ve ever lived.” Thus, Joshua Tree is not an “isolated” and “independent” desert town fighting off predatory global forces, but rather a product of regional and national flows that create a unique intersection attractive to tourists. And these tourists, largely travelling to the area by personal vehicle, are contributing to the very global greenhouse emissions that solar development, with all its problems, would curb.

## **Opportunities**

The town of Joshua Tree will transform as the impacts of global climate change become more apparent. At the front lines are the iconic Joshua Trees, arguably one of the main features drawing tourists to Joshua Tree National Park. The loss of Joshua Trees runs the risk of increasing economic instability in the region. And despite widespread national and regional support for alternative energy and solar power, residents largely oppose local projects. This is due to permitting issues, rapidly changing technology, distrust of large corporations, a lack of visible impacts from climate change, and local utopianism. The stalemate seems ironic, irreconcilable, and tragic.

Is there an environmental ethic that could transcend the recurring solar stalemate in a place like Joshua Tree? How might Massey’s “global sense of place” be realized? And ultimately, could this ethic lend itself to addressing global environmental problems like climate change as well as preserving the uniqueness of place that occurs when local, regional, national, and global flows intersect? Ursula Heise (2008) suggests replacing traditional place-based environmentalism with eco-cosmopolitanism, which explicitly recognizes the modern and global context in which environmental challenges are rooted. To Heise, both the reflexive rejection of the global and the simplistic recognition that “everything is connected” do little to provide workable frameworks for moving forward. Hayden (2010) speaks to this in his argument that social and environmental justice must be applied globally, with attention to individuals rather than at the state scale. The embrace of eco-cosmopolitanism means that benefitting from national and global networks also entails a responsibility towards them. Rather than pit the rapacious global against the innocent local, the two must be seen as mutually shaping and reinforcing each other. Perhaps within an eco-cosmopolitan framework, the development of alternative energy in the Joshua Tree region could, at minimum, be one of dialogue and engagement.
